title: The Komagata Maru, 1914
hook: a ship of mostly Sikh passengers is turned away at Vancouver and returns to violence in India

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stockton: the first gurdwara in the United States, the Guru's door, and your line, a door in a new land. Today, a door that stayed shut, and a ship that waited in front of it for two months. Day three hundred sixteen.

May 1914. A Japanese steamship sails into Vancouver harbor, its rails lined with men in turbans, looking at the city. Three hundred seventy-six passengers, most of them Sikh, all of them British subjects, the same empire as Canada. They've come to work, like the mill men before them. The ship drops anchor. And then nothing happens. Nobody is allowed off. Days pass. Then weeks. The city watches from the shore. Today: the Komagata Maru.
screen: `MAY 1914, VANCOUVER HARBOR.` → `376 PASSENGERS, MOSTLY SIKH.` → `NOBODY IS ALLOWED OFF.`

segments.voice: Remember the rule that closed Canada's door: immigrants had to arrive by a continuous journey from home, and no ships ran straight from India. A Sikh businessman named Gurdit Singh decided to test it. He chartered a ship, the Komagata Maru, and filled it with passengers from Punjab. He even gave it a new name: Guru Nanak Jahaz, the Guru Nanak ship. When it reached Vancouver, the authorities refused to let the passengers land. The ship sat in the harbor for two months. Food and water ran low. The Sikhs of Vancouver, those mill workers, raised money to help and fought in the courts. They lost. Only about twenty passengers, mostly returning residents, were allowed in. In July, with a navy ship standing by, the Komagata Maru was forced to sail away. The story doesn't end there. When the ship reached India, near Calcutta, in September 1914, British police met it. The passengers were ordered onto a train to Punjab; many refused. There was a confrontation, shots were fired, and around twenty passengers were killed. Others were imprisoned. For decades, Sikhs in Canada kept the memory alive: plaques, books, a memorial on the Vancouver waterfront. In 2016, Canada's Prime Minister stood in the House of Commons and apologized for what was done. Why does it matter now? Because they were turned away not for anything they did, but for who they were and where they were from. The memorial on the Vancouver waterfront stands near where the ship once waited.
screen: `TESTING A CLOSED DOOR.` · `TWO MONTHS IN THE HARBOR.` · `SHOTS NEAR CALCUTTA.` · `AN APOLOGY, 2016.` · then, large: `THEY WERE TURNED AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare to welcome one newcomer. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone new in your life: a new neighbor, a new coworker, a new kid in class, someone who just joined a group you're in. Picture what it's like to be them right now, standing at the edge, not sure if they're wanted. Then picture yourself walking over. What's the one simple thing you'd say? Rehearse it quietly. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The Komagata Maru. In 1914, a ship of mostly Sikh passengers waited two months at Vancouver, was turned away, and met violence on its return to India.
Your line: they were turned away. Today, welcome one newcomer, with a name, a question or a seat beside you. Day three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs in Canada remember the Komagata Maru each year, with Ardas and gatherings at the Vancouver memorial, and tell the story to their children as part of the community's history.

fork.setup: you're Gurdit Singh in 1914. Canada says immigrants must come by a continuous journey, and no such ships run from India. what do you do?
options: accept the rule and stay home.
charter a ship and sail straight to Vancouver.
go to the United States instead.
fork.reveal: he chartered the Komagata Maru to test the rule. the passengers were still refused, and the ship was forced away.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Guru Nanak jahaz, the Guru Nanak ship, Gurdit Singh's name for the Komagata Maru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ship was denied entry because of paperwork.
what it means: people were turned away for who they were, and many met violence on their return.
what a scholar hears: 376 passengers arrived on May 23, 1914; the ship left on July 23; about twenty were killed at Budge Budge on September 29, 1914.

sources.ref: Apology in the House of Commons of Canada, May 18, 2016

notes: Passenger count (376; commonly 340 Sikhs, 24 Muslims, 12 Hindus), dates (arrival May 23, departure July 23, Budge Budge September 29, 1914) and deaths (about 19–20 passengers) are the commonly given figures; confirm.
Gurdit Singh's renaming of the ship as Guru Nanak Jahaz and the Gurmukhi spelling: confirm.
